newsitem.title: AUSTRIA: Austrian opposition unites to boycott parliament.
newsitem.headline: Austrian opposition unites to boycott parliament.

text.p: Austria's normally fractious opposition said on Thursday it was boycotting parliament in a last-ditch effort to force an inquiry into the Vienna slaying of three Kurdish activists, thought to be by Iranian hitmen.

The leftist Greens, Liberals and far-right Freedom Party, frustrated by their inability to win a parliamentary vote on the issue, announced at a joint news conference they would block all committee proceedings until June 10.
"We have overcome our ideological differences to agree on this emergency measure," Ewald Stadler, deputy whip of the Freedom Party, told reporters.

The opposition is calling for an all-party inquiry into allegations that ministers stifled a police investigation into the slaying of Iranian Kurdish leader Abdorrahman Qasemlu and two other activists in Vienna eight years ago.

Former Iranian president Abolhassan Bani-Sadr and a former top official at the Austrian foreign ministry have backed claims that the government buckled under economic and political pressure from Tehran and allowed the suspects to flee.
The government has conceded Iran tried to force its hand but denied it gave way.

"The opposition has already made four attempts to force the government to set up a parliamentary committee but each time it has failed because of the government's majority," the three opposition parties said in a statement.
The bloc holds 60 seats in the 183-seat assembly, dominated by Chancellor Viktor Klima's Social Democrats and Foreign Minister Wolfgang Schuessel's conservative People's Party.

"The government can withdraw into the fortress of its parliamentary majority if it so wishes. We will at least have succeeded in getting our message across to the electorate," Liberal whip Hans Peter Haselsteiner told Reuters.

He said the parties would review their uneasy alliance after June 10 and decide on their next move. The Liberals, born out of an acrimonious split in the Freedom Party in 1993, are normally at loggerheads with the far right along with the Greens.

The government condemned the boycott as anti-democratic and insisted it would not allow it to affect parliamentary business. Parliamentary committees would continue to meet with or without opposition members, it insisted.

"It is up to the parliamentary majority to decide who is right. We cannot allow a group with a minority of less than one third to force parliament's hand," People's Party whip Andreas Khol told Austrian radio.
Last week the government published its own 200-page report into its handling of the Kurd murder investigation which exonerated ministers from any wrongdoing.
Austrian opposition parties and the domestic media have slammed the paper and called it a whitewash.
